THE LOST COAST OF LOUISIANA

A landscape slowly disappearing
02 / 12
“Some places disappear because people leave them. Others disappear because the land itself is leaving.”
03 / 12

For thousands of years, the river built Louisiana.

Every flood carried sediment. Every flood created new land.

04 / 12

Marshes. Bayous. Barrier islands. Swamps.

The coastline is alive, flexible, always moving.

05 / 12

Once the river was leveed, its sediment stopped reaching the wetlands.

The very engineering that protected communities also changed how new land was created.

06 / 12

The land itself is sinking.

Subsidence now combines with other pressures to speed the loss.

07 / 12

Storms and shifting channels reshape the coast.

The coastline never returns exactly as it was.

08 / 12

For the people who live here, this isn’t an environmental issue. It’s home.

Shrimpers. Oystermen. Tribal communities. Commercial fishermen.

09 / 12

Isle de Jean Charles. Delacroix. Shell Beach. Grand Chenier.

These aren’t just names on a map. They’re chapters of Louisiana’s history.

10 / 12

One of the world’s largest coastal restoration efforts is underway here.

Sediment diversions. Marsh creation. Barrier island restoration.

11 / 12

The coast isn’t only home to people.

Birds. Alligators. Fish. Shrimp. Migratory species.

12 / 12

The coast isn’t gone. It is changing.

The question is what we choose to protect, restore, and pass on.
